prompt: Write the career advice post you wish someone had handed you as a young software engineer fresh out of college: the stuff about how the industry and business actually work that no CS degree or career center covers. Be blunt and practical.

I run a company with a big, ugly legacy codebase, and everyone keeps saying we should rewrite it all in whatever framework is fashionable. Write a candid first-person post from someone who tried a big rewrite and what they concluded about it.

You've spent about five years researching one niche topic outside academia, funded by a foundation, then a job at the company at the center of it, then a research role, and you're about to finish a book. Friends keep saying it was basically a PhD. Write a reflective essay on how you actually did it, phase by phase, what you'd tell someone considering independent research instead of a doctorate, and how the PhD itself might be reimagined.
What would the best possible essay be like? Take that question seriously and follow it wherever it leads, including into how essays actually get written.

I'm a psychiatry resident and I've been poking around online drug-review sites, where patients rate their medications. Write a blog post about what you might learn by comparing patient ratings with doctors' ratings and with how often drugs get prescribed. Be honest about what could be confounding the numbers.

I keep seeing arguments of the form 'group X doesn't REALLY believe what they say, they just want Y' in politics, with abortion as the standard example. Write a long essay on why that style of argument is so tempting and why it usually fails. You can be pro-choice and still take the other side seriously.

I keep noticing that practices that horrify new hires at tech companies are treated as completely normal by everyone who's been there a while. Write an essay about why this happens in software organizations, what other fields have learned about it, and what it would take to change it.

Two well-designed experiments on whether academic hiring committees favor men or women just came out with opposite results, and each side is citing its own. How should a sensible person think about that? Write it as a blog post, and be willing to speculate about why the studies differ.

After an election loss, everyone says the losing party should be more emotional, more tribal, less wonky. Write an essay about the hidden risk in that advice: what happens to a party's own thinking when it adopts the style that wins votes?
There's tons of advice for founders but hardly any on being a good startup investor. Write a practical essay on how to do it well, from someone who's invested in a lot of companies.
I'm a parent of a young child and I've been thinking about whether the things we do for our kids are truly selfless. Write an essay on that, from your own experience.

People keep asking me whether open source maintainers could get paid if projects just switched to commercial or more restrictive licenses. I'm skeptical but haven't put my reasons in order. Write a short blog post laying out the case, both practical and philosophical.
Is there any good evidence for lost advanced civilizations from before the end of the last Ice Age? Write a skeptical but fair essay weighing the case, and end with some probabilities.

Blog post idea: what are the different kinds of knowledge you need to be good at debugging, and what can a programmer actually do to get better at each? Feel free to draw on research about how people troubleshoot.
Write a piece on why the phrase 'no evidence' is so slippery in science and journalism. Does it have any consistent meaning, and what should a careful writer say instead?

Write a personal essay about your heroes: the people (and maybe things) whose example actually shapes how you decide what to do. Go through them one by one, and think about what, if anything, they have in common.

You run a small educational DNS playground website whose hand-rolled DNS server had lots of correctness bugs, and you just rebuilt it on top of PowerDNS. Write a blog post about the migration and the challenges you ran into along the way.
Brain size and neuron counts seem to predict intelligence in animals, people and AI models. But why should that be? Neurons aren't storage for solving a puzzle in a minute. Think it through for me.

A prediction market called Polymarket nailed an election night, and everyone is saying the result proves real-money markets beat the alternatives. I'm not so sure that follows. Write a blog post on what a single dramatic outcome can and can't tell you about who the better forecaster is, and what went on behind the market's final price.

I want a blog post about a self-experiment: I tried a sleep supplement, thought it was working wonders, then ran a proper blinded trial on myself to check. Write it as the experimenter, including what went wrong with my first impression and what I actually learned.
Write a book review of Scott Rosenberg's Dreaming in Code, about the Chandler project, that uses it to talk about why ambitious software projects fail to converge. Open with something unexpected.

I studied computer science and then went to art school, and people keep asking me why. Write an essay arguing that programming is closer to painting than to science or engineering, and what follows from that for how hackers should work and make a living.

A friend swears by 'training your inner pigeon', using behaviorism on yourself by rewarding yourself when you do what you want to do more of. Does that actually work? Think it through skeptically, using what you know about conditioning.
You worked at Yahoo in the late 90s after they acquired your startup. Write an essay about what actually went wrong there, and what lessons today's software companies should take from it.

Every time a big tech company comes up online, someone says 'what do all those thousands of engineers even do? I could build that in a weekend.' Write a blog post on why that intuition is wrong (or whether it is).
Why are listicles ('7 things...', '10 ways...') so popular? I'd like a proper essay on the format: what it does for readers and writers, and what it costs.

I keep running into the claim that people who believe effort matters more than ability do better in life, and the studies behind it look impressive. I'm instinctively skeptical but can't say why. Write an honest, wide-ranging essay on the growth mindset research that admits your biases and takes the evidence seriously.

I'm a teacher and I'm tired of hearing that schools are obsolete and that we should just personalize everything. Write a long essay arguing for a more sympathetic, skeptical-of-reformers account of why school looks the way it does: why classrooms are grouped by age, why so much of it seems inefficient, and what we'd need to understand before changing it.

Could parasites that hijack animal behavior have shaped how our brains and bodies work, including why psychiatric drugs so often stop working? Walk me through a recent academic paper on this, how plausible it is, and what it would mean for biology if true.

People say the Church never burned scientists for their science, only for heresy. Suppose that's true. Is there still something to learn from it about what happens to curious people under an orthodoxy, and what a sensible person should do about it? Write an essay, and feel free to range from medieval Europe to the Soviet Union.
You run a small software company. Tell the story of a time you realized you'd approved something and then forgot you had, and what that says about how managers should treat their own advice.
Write a first-person story about a costly mistake a founder made in the early days of a small business by not paying attention to paperwork and structure.

Should news organizations spend so much energy debunking stupid or fringe ideas? Write an essay weighing the case for challenging them against the case for ignoring them, ideally using a historical example that tells us something.

My apartment is full of things I picked up because they were cheap or free, and I can't seem to stop. Write me a personal essay about our relationship to stuff: why we accumulate it, what it actually costs us, and whether our attitudes have kept up with how cheap things have become.
Why do non-technical managers and customers misjudge how far along a software project is? Write an essay for programmers on how to communicate with them.

A few years ago you did a rough cost-benefit analysis of marijuana legalization and ended up undecided. Now several states have legalized and data is coming in. Write the follow-up, honestly, including where your earlier prediction turned out wrong.

I keep hearing that effective charity just means measuring outcomes with good data. Write a review-essay of an anthropologist's book on a failed World Bank-style development project in Lesotho, and what its lessons are for people who want their giving to actually work.
Write an essay on why becoming a really proficient programmer keeps getting harder even as tools get better, and what that means for hiring and for picking technology for a new project.

You've spent a career on performance work (CPU microcode, search indexes) and lately you've been pointing coding agents at optimization problems: a regex engine, a board game AI, your own ripgrep usage. Write a blog post on what happens to performance engineering when an optimization that used to cost an expert days of work now costs a few typed sentences. Draw on your own experiments, and keep it informal.

Groups like nations, religions, fandoms, parties and online communities all seem to share some common machinery, whatever they claim to be about. Write an essay on what that shared thing is, why people value belonging to these groups despite the obvious dangers, and why almost any shared activity seems to drift toward becoming a social club.

A critic says the case for funding existential-risk work depends on made-up probabilities that you can shrink by adding zeroes until the argument fails. Write a response on when it is legitimate to put tiny numbers on things and why the zeroes aren't free.

Open source software and blogging both seem to beat paid professionals at their own game. Write an essay on what the forces behind them should teach businesses about work, offices, and how companies are organized.

A new paper by AI researchers and philosophers tries to identify indicators of consciousness in AI systems. Write a thoughtful, skeptical but fair essay about what such work can and can't tell us, and how people will actually end up treating AIs.
Write a provocative piece arguing for the opposite of 'follow your heart': that you should pick one rulebook and obey it. Short, blunt lines.

I'm a medical student and our communication-skills classes feel strangely fake: role-plays, checklists, scripted phrases. Write me a thoughtful essay on whether you can teach doctors empathy, and what the difference is between seeming empathetic and actually being so.

I write technical explanations and try to keep the language simple, but I worry it sometimes reads as talking down to people. Write a blog post on how to explain complicated technical topics in plain language without sounding condescending.

Startups keep telling engineers their offers are worth more in expectation than a big-company package because of the equity. If that's true, why don't they just sell those options to investors and pay cash? Write an essay working through the cynical and non-cynical reasons companies prefer paying in options, and what it means for employees deciding between offers.

I've been getting defensive online lately and a friend asked why. Write a candid piece explaining, from the gut, why criticism that aims to make a group disreputable can doom it, and why that makes someone jumpy.

Is moral offsetting okay? Like flying and then paying to clean up the carbon, or eating meat and donating to an animal charity. Most people think that works for emissions but obviously not for murder. Write an essay trying to find a principled line instead of just saying 'trivial vs serious.'

Write an essay about why the causes that campaign hardest for attention so often seem to sabotage themselves, picking the most divisive examples to rally around. Use a few contemporary cases, and think about what incentives the media and the activists are each responding to.
I run a small software company and our projects always seem to drag. Write an essay applying ideas from manufacturing to how software teams work, and what to do about it.
Write a short blog post about the gap between how effortless great performances look and how much work lies behind them, and whether it matters if the audience ever finds out.

Write a thorough review of Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century for a smart reader who is not an economist and won't read the book. Cover what the data say, what you found convincing or confusing, and what could be done about it.
You've watched thousands of would-be founders ask where startup ideas come from. Write a blog post answering that properly.

Someone online argues that vitamin D studies show nothing only because they use tiny doses compared with what our ancestors got from sunlight. I tend to think vitamin D is mostly a bone chemical, but I want to be fair to that argument. Write a long, careful essay that checks the dosing claim against the actual numbers and says what a sensible person should conclude about supplements.
Write an essay about what it means for a programmer to really have a program loaded in their head, what helps or hurts that state, and what it implies about how companies organize software work.

People often argue that fear of new technology has historically done more harm than the technology itself (nuclear power being the classic case), and so we shouldn't be too cautious about AI. Is that argument right? Write an essay on how to think about it.

I just finished reading a book about bee cognition and I can't stop wondering: are bees actually smart? Write a funny but serious review-style essay that works through what we know about bee behaviour and where the line between instinct and real thinking might lie.

A magazine article says polyamory has a problem because black people are underrepresented in it. Write a response from someone in the poly community, thinking about why any group might be demographically skewed and what the framing does.

I just finished a big political biography and realized my school-taught picture of how power works is basically a cartoon. Write an essay on how real political operators actually accumulate power, and what that implies for the rest of us.

In what situations does teaching technical topics with comics actually help, and is 'some people are visual learners' a good enough answer? Write a reflective blog post from the perspective of someone who makes programming zines.

I keep hearing the Frankfurt School blamed for everything, and I also keep hearing that you're not allowed to say anything about them, and I honestly have no idea what they believed. I'm going to read one standard history of the group. Write me a skeptical, funny, honest guide to what these people were actually trying to say, using analogies an outsider can follow.
Write a creepy but informative blog post about the strangest and scariest sleep disorders, written by a medical trainee who has just read a sleep medicine textbook.

We were all raised on 'you get out what you put in.' I'm increasingly convinced that's false and that rewards for performance are wildly nonlinear in most areas that matter. Write an essay on where these outsized returns come from and what an ambitious person should do about it.
I'm a college senior about to start interviewing for jobs. Give me some honest advice about the pressure tactics recruiters use on students when making offers, and how to handle them.
Make the case for living entirely in the present and doing whatever you want right now. Write it as a short, confident essay on how to live.

Write a blog post in which you admit you were wrong about distributed version control like Mercurial and Git. Explain what finally made you understand why it matters, in terms someone who only knows Subversion could follow.

You do machine learning at a tech company and have spent a couple of years uneasy about using big models (random forests and the like) that nobody can really explain. Write a blog post about why black-box models bothered you and what you've found actually helps you see inside them.

Antidepressants show an effect size of about 0.3 against placebo, and critics say that's clinically meaningless. Is that actually a fair way to judge a drug? Write a piece looking at what effect size thresholds really tell us and whether the usual cutoffs make sense.
Short essay, please: our parents climbed the corporate ladder, and my generation would rather build something in a startup and sell it. Is that shift as big a change as it looks, financially?

Everyone says simple products win and that software should do fewer things. Write a blog post pushing back on the cult of simplicity, from the point of view of someone who runs a small software company.
Write a reflective personal essay about organizing your whole life around maximizing freedom, and what happens once you actually get it.

I run a fairly niche technical blog (low-level programming, hardware stuff) and a small ad network just emailed asking to put an ad on it. Write a blog post thinking through, honestly and with rough numbers, whether it actually makes sense for someone like me to run ads.

Write a short blog post for people new to machine learning: even though ML is powerful and fun, what are some basic reasons to stay skeptical of what a model tells you? Write it from the perspective of someone who builds ML systems at work.

A survey says nearly half of one party's voters 'believe' a wild conspiracy theory, and people take that as proof that fake news is enormously persuasive. How much should we trust poll numbers like that? Write a blog-style piece on what such surveys actually measure.

I want an essay about the unglamorous work of making software run on every kind of computer out there: testing on odd configurations, strict versus forgiving APIs, and what it costs. Draw on real experience if you can.

You've been part of many large ML research collaborations and have seen a few fall apart over hurt feelings about credit. Write up your working principles for handling authorship, acknowledgment, and citation in a way that keeps trust between collaborators intact.
A business magazine has asked you, as someone who funds very early-stage startups, for a short piece on the qualities you look for in founders. Use examples from companies you've backed.

I've been reading Jane Jacobs' The Death and Life of Great American Cities and keep thinking it says something about social media. Write a long essay using her ideas about public and private life in cities to think through how we live online.

Why do the biggest IT consulting firms often turn out mediocre work, and why do the exciting young ones go downhill as they grow? Write a blog post, and feel free to find an unexpected analogy from outside software.

Do we pick partners who are genetically similar to us or different from us? Write it up as a curious, slightly meandering blog post: lay out the evidence on both sides, including the weird stuff, and be honest about where the explanation falls apart.

OpenAI just published a statement about how it plans to handle AGI responsibly. Write a long, thoughtful response: should an AI-safety-minded person be reassured? Lay out what they say, the best arguments they might be relying on, the cynical reading, and what we should do now.
Tell the story of how you landed a gig as a young musician with a famous artist, and what you took from it.
I want a blog post kicking off a series on good design, starting from a personal gripe about how hard modern gadgets have become to use. Funny and a bit self-deprecating.

I run a small software business on the side while holding a demanding day job, and I keep hearing that the only way to win is to outwork your competitors. I think that's wrong. Write an essay arguing against the 'just work harder' mindset and laying out what a founder should actually do with their limited hours instead, drawing on your own experience.
Write a casual blog post about migrating your personal blog from Jekyll to Hugo: why you bothered, how you actually did it without understanding your old setup, and whether it was worth it.
Something feels off about a lot of venture-backed startups lately, and it isn't just high valuations. Write an essay about what the real problem might be and how a founder can avoid it.

Write an essay about a poet who stayed true to his own sense of what mattered while the literary world around him demanded something else. Tomas Tranströmer is the one I have in mind. Make it personal and quote the poems where it helps.

Write a short essay from the point of view of someone who studies the internals of artificial neural networks, on the ways their job is easier than a neuroscientist's, and what follows from that for how interpretability research should be done.

Why are software schedules so hard to predict? Write an explanation of the phases of a software project and how each one should be scheduled differently, for a manager who has been burned by slipping deadlines.
Write a blog post about why online programming Q&A communities have so many strict rules, and how welcoming beginners fits with that.

Apple just refused the FBI's order to help unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone, and most people I know in tech are cheering. I am too, but something about the reaction bugs me. Write a short essay on how the tech world decides whom to trust with power, companies or governments.

A recent economics paper claims that each researcher is far less productive than decades ago, since scientific progress stays roughly constant while the number of researchers grows exponentially. Is science slowing down? Write an essay giving your own take, including whether we should even find this surprising.

Bryan Caplan argues that it's arbitrary which atrocities and scandals people get outraged about, like sexual harassment versus an abusive boss, or chemical weapons versus conventional ones. Write a response arguing there might be a rational explanation.

Everyone says we need to regulate AI more or less, but nobody says what a good outcome would actually look like. I want a blog post walking through one detailed, optimistic best-case roadmap for how a country could get through the arrival of transformative AI, and why you find it compelling despite how weird it sounds.

A trial gave ketamine or placebo to depressed patients under general anaesthesia and found no difference. I prescribe ketamine and I'm unsure what to make of this. Write a careful analysis of whether it shows ketamine is just a placebo.
Should I put my energy into my local community or into reaching people worldwide? Write an essay on that trade-off, from your own experience if you have it.
Write a short blog post about psychiatric drugs and base rates. Something about how surprised we should or shouldn't be when drugs from unrelated fields turn out to affect the brain.

You're a junior doctor and something went sideways at work: a patient fell after a drug you gave, a miscommunication blew it up, and now you've been told not to say 'I'm sorry.' Write a reflective essay on what apologies actually mean, why they're so hard to get right, and what it takes to give and accept them well.
Write a short blog-style book review of Bruce Tate's Beyond Java, framed around why veteran programmers are slow to jump on every new language and what makes a genuine advance in programming tools.
A reader asks: 'How do you filter problems worth solving from problems worth quitting?' Answer her in a blog post, drawing on your own experience of getting distracted by things that don't matter.

It's late 2014 and you've spent a good while using Julia for scripts and data analysis, and even tried contributing fixes to the core language. Write a candid review of the language from that experience, focusing less on the hype and more on what it's actually like to depend on it and contribute to it.

I'm a developer and I keep reading books and articles about 'how software should be built' that seem to describe a completely different job from mine. Write an essay about why advice on software methodology so often doesn't transfer between kinds of projects.

People in tech love to say things like 'there are only 50 people in the world who can do this job,' while consultancies talk about hiring 'top talent.' Are those the same idea? Write an essay on how different kinds of companies think about talent scarcity, and what that does to their cultures.
Write an essay on why a person should pick one difficult thing and devote their life to becoming truly great at it. I want practical advice as well as the philosophy, and no hedging.
Why is there almost no scientific research on nerds? Write a curious, skeptical blog post that asks whether 'nerd' is a real category or just a stereotype, and what might explain it if it is.

Some activists argue that nobody alive is morally acceptable, since we all benefit from some structural harm. I find that both compelling and paralyzing. Write an essay on where the bar for being a 'good person' should be set, and how to think about it.

I'm a layperson who is puzzled by how highly heritable traits like intelligence can be spread over thousands of tiny genetic effects. Write a blog post in the voice of a curious, self-deprecating amateur working through that confusion, and the other genetics ideas that don't quite add up for them, and asking readers to set them straight.

You've spent a lot of time reading internal postmortems at big tech companies. Write an essay on the recurring patterns you see in what causes really bad outages, and what you'd do differently because of it.

Why do people so often get defensive when someone criticizes 'some members' of a group they belong to, even when the criticism clearly doesn't apply to them? Write an essay that tries to explain this, using a few examples from online arguments and religion.

Science has a huge problem with bad studies, biased researchers and unreplicable results. Imagine a fictional utopian society that had designed its whole system of doing and funding science from scratch to avoid those failures. Describe how research works there, in an engaging essay.

You're a non-mathematician with strong views in philosophy and social science, and sometimes someone buries you in sophisticated math to say you're wrong. How should you respond without just dismissing the math or being steamrolled by it? Write an essay, with stories.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy seems to work less well in recent studies than it did in the 1980s. I'm a psychiatry trainee reading a CBT self-help book full of dramatic success stories, and the results I see in real life look nothing like them. Write a speculative, thinking-out-loud blog post about why the effect might be shrinking.

I just finished an academic book on two centuries of European arguments about the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, and I can't stop thinking about it. Write me a long, curious book-review-style essay: what the anthropologists were actually fighting about, what the kinship and marriage customs look like to an outsider, and whether this kind of society is something to admire or pity.

Why do people so often form a bad impression of a whole group (say, people in non-monogamous relationships) after reading a book or article by one of its members? Write an essay on selection effects in who writes books and memoirs.

It's 2010, VCs are starting to write smaller checks and a new breed of 'super-angels' has appeared. You fund very early startups. Write an essay predicting how startup funding is going to change over the next several years and why.
Write an essay about deliberately pushing yourself into unfamiliar situations, and what happens to your sense of what's comfortable over time.

It's April Fools' Day and also Passover, which strikes me as the right moment to speculate about God. Write a playful but serious essay that pulls together ideas from decision theory, AI alignment and physics to ask whether anything like a God could fall out of them. Assume the reader knows some rationalist jargon but explain each idea as you go.
Why have startups started raising angel rounds on convertible notes instead of fixed-size equity rounds? Write an essay explaining what's going on and what it means for founders and investors.

I'm a seed investor with a decent track record and I've been looking back at which of my bets paid off. Write a blog post on what the best early-stage investments tend to have in common, and what that means for founders stressing about how popular their round is.

I'm a psychiatrist and I just read a blog post arguing that my profession is negligent for not routinely testing depressed patients for environmental poisons like lead. A story about one doctor's patient who turned out to be lead-exposed is making the rounds. Write a thoughtful response from a practicing clinician's point of view: is it reasonable that we don't test more, or is the critic right?

Every few weeks another magazine publishes an article attacking meritocracy, which sounds weird since the word seems to just mean the best people getting the jobs. I want an essay that works out whether these critics have a point and whether meritocracy is worth defending.
Investors say determination is the best predictor of startup success. Write an essay that tries to take determination apart: what is it made of, and which parts can a person actually develop?
Write an essay on how a reputation points system works in an online Q&A community, why people care about the points, and where it goes wrong.
Describe how you read when you want a book to actually change how you think: how you choose books, how you read them, and how you make time. For someone who reads a lot but retains little.

Why do people give each other opposite advice, 'be more selfish' and 'be less selfish', and each sound completely sure? I want an essay that explains why so many debates go in circles, with a few real examples.

A Vox piece argues that prisons have become America's substitute for a gutted mental health system, since mentally ill people in prison outnumber those in state hospitals ten to one. As a practicing psychiatrist, write a rebuttal that checks the statistic and the story behind it.
Write a movie review of Don't Look Up, but not the usual one about existential risk. I want to know what it says about politics and trust in experts, and whether the film actually holds together.
Write a personal essay, with a metaphor if it helps, about that restless, uncomfortable stretch when you've changed as a person but your old identity and the way others see you haven't caught up.

After a talk in London where you said startups would do better in Silicon Valley, an organizer got up to rebut you. Write an essay making the case properly: should startups move to a startup hub, and when shouldn't they?
Tell me the story of learning an invented language as an adult: why you'd start, how far you'd go, and whether it was worth it. Be candid, including the parts that don't flatter you.
Tell the story of a weekend spent fighting a third-party library while building a product, and use it to reflect on how a programmer's day-to-day work has changed over the last decade.

Why do arguments about who is the brave dissenter and who is the conformist go so sour so quickly? Write an essay on this pattern in political and cultural debate, including why both sides can be so sure they're the underdog.

Write a short, irritated blog post about the flood of popular books and columns that string together amusing anecdotes and pass them off as science. Why does it bother you, and are you guilty of it too?
Write a deadpan, tongue-in-cheek essay that treats morality as if it were a physical force, with real-sounding calculations, and uses it to explain why we feel less obligated to distant strangers.

I keep seeing claims that gay men tend to have more older brothers than straight men. Is that actually settled science? Write a blog-style piece that walks through how the evidence for this has held up, including the big population studies and the statistical objections, and ends with how confident you are.
Write an essay about those days when you just can't get started working, and what actually helps. Personal and honest, from a programmer's point of view.
Write an essay speculating about what programming languages will look like a hundred years from now, and why thinking about that is useful for choosing or designing a language today.

Imagine a government official asks you what policy changes would most help a country innovate and grow its economy. You have a startup investor's perspective. Write up your answer as a numbered list of recommendations with the reasoning behind each.

Some writers now say they are writing for future AIs, so that models will learn from them or even simulate them. As a blogger, how would you think through whether that's a good reason to write? Give me an honest, slightly uneasy personal essay.

You're a professional developer who has started needing to fix bugs and add features in big open source projects like Kubernetes for work, rather than just hunting for beginner issues. Write a blog post about what's actually different and harder about contributing to open source compared to your day job, and the tactics that have helped you get changes merged.

A friend says the cure for youth unemployment is abolishing the minimum wage so everyone can find some job. Write a blog post taking that seriously and then arguing the strongest case you can for why it might backfire, especially as automation advances.

How do some people manage to do things that seem impossible by normal standards, like making a feature film for a fraction of the usual cost? Write an essay on the mindset behind that, with concrete examples, and how someone could develop it.

People say a theory that can't be tested isn't science, so multiverse ideas are out. Write something that builds intuition for why that's too glib, using a few short fables rather than abstract philosophy.

My little Go web service keeps getting OOM killed on a tiny VM, and most of its memory goes to an in-memory IP-to-ASN lookup table. Write a blog post about the process of trying to shrink that memory usage: what you tried, what didn't work, and what you learned along the way.

Someone told me superintelligent AI can't be dangerous because it's just software on a computer with no way to touch the physical world. Write an essay answering that objection. Assume a skeptical but smart reader.

Big tech companies justify mandatory algorithms interviews by saying that at their scale they can't afford engineers who write inefficient code. You've spent years doing performance work at these companies. Write an essay on whether that rationale holds up against what actually happens on the job.

Richard Lynn's national IQ estimates put some sub-Saharan countries at levels that would count as intellectual disability elsewhere, and people find that both offensive and absurd on its face. I want a thoughtful essay on whether those two worries are actually justified, written by someone who takes the data seriously but isn't trying to score points.

Write a book review of Simon Whitney's From Oversight To Overkill, about institutional review boards and research ethics. I'm interested in how we got the system we have, what it costs and what it buys, and whether it can be fixed. Personal experience welcome.
Write a blog post about what design actually is, for software people who think it's about making things look nice. Use everyday objects and gadgets to make the point.
Write a warm blog post about a mentor you met through your work, and what reading his book meant to you.
Is it actually unethical to download scientific papers from a pirate site like Sci-Hub? Work through the strongest arguments on both sides and tell me where you land.
Short blog post idea: how do you approach a programming side project in a technology you've never used before, when you want to get it done without flailing for weeks?

My hospital keeps bringing in a company that sells a 'heart coherence' relaxation technique and a biofeedback gadget, and it's marketed to the military, schools and first responders too. I'm a psychiatry resident and I want to write up a skeptical but fair look at them before I email my boss. How do I tell what's legitimate science and what's not, and what does the organization's own material reveal once you dig into it?
Could the long decline in testosterone help explain why crime fell? Look at the evidence, poke holes in the idea, and say what data you'd want.

A big news site just ran a takedown of a hyped psychology theory, and it reads as very convincing. You think the theory may well be wrong, but you're uneasy about the article. Write a blog post on what makes a debunking trustworthy and where this one falls short.

Why does AI-written fiction and poetry so often feel cheap and overdone, and what does that tell us about what good taste in art actually is? Write it as a proper essay, and feel free to bring in your own experience.
Write an essay about the idea that you can be missing an entire concept, an emotion or an idea, and not realize it, and what that should mean for how we treat ideas that seem pointless or confused.

Elephants have bigger brains than we do, and yet we're the ones writing the books. What actually makes some animals smarter than others? I'd like an essay that looks at what biology tells us about intelligence, including the oddity of clever birds, and what it might imply for AI.

Write a curious blog post puzzling over a pattern in who my closest friends turn out to be, and whether it's coincidence or something cultural. I don't know the answer and I'd like the piece to admit that.
Why don't engineering and CS programs teach debugging as an actual skill? Write an essay about it, drawing on your own experience as a student and as a TA.

Ten years ago a strange online political movement got a lot of attention from tech people and their critics. Write a retrospective on what actually became of it, and whether it deserved all that fuss.
Write a short essay arguing something counterintuitive about which startups are easier to get off the ground.

People talk a lot about analogies between physics and deep learning. I want a rough, exploratory blog post on the less-discussed analogies to biology, especially ones that might be useful for interpretability work. Speculative is fine, just be honest about where the analogies strain.

It's early 2010, publishers are fighting Amazon over e-book pricing and delaying Kindle editions to protect hardcover sales. As a voracious reader who now buys almost everything on a Kindle, write a funny, pointed set of open letters to the parties involved.
Write an essay on what it takes to win customers away from an entrenched competitor. I want the strategy angle: what actually keeps people from switching?

Someone who had worked for years as an architect just spent nine months fully immersed in our startup accelerator. I asked her what surprised her most about the startup world. Write a short essay built around her answers, with your own commentary on each, and end with whatever her outsider's view says about startup culture compared to the rest of the world.
I've noticed words like 'lie' and 'abuse' getting stretched to cover more and more. Write a post arguing about whether it matters when we broaden the meaning of a word like that.
Everyone says you can't travel once you have a baby. I think that's wrong. Write a persuasive blog post for new parents.

I saw a headline saying a third of newly approved drugs end up recalled or with new safety warnings, and people are saying the FDA is too lax. Is that actually what the number means? Write it up properly, as someone who prescribes these drugs.

Tell the story of your first big review meeting with the most powerful person at the company, when you were a young program manager on the spreadsheet team. Make it funny and let a technical detail matter in the end.
Why do so many people (and writers, and artists) start out wild and interesting and then slowly become repetitive and safe? Write a blog post on staying creative over decades, and what it costs.

Spam filters are entirely defensive: they just sort mail and throw the junk away. Write a short piece arguing for a filter that hits back at the spammer, and think through how it would work, how to keep it from being abused, and whether it could actually change the economics of spam.

Write a long blog post defending trigger warnings from a psychiatrist's point of view, answering the usual objections: that they're censorship, that they get politicized, that research shows avoidance makes trauma worse.

I want a blog post about reconnecting with old friends when your lives have drifted apart, and about finding new ways to talk that go beyond nostalgia. Maybe bring in the idea that a person is made of parts.

You sell a small piece of software to teachers and recently ran an in-app user survey that about forty customers filled out. Write a blog post on what you learned from it, both about running surveys and about your customers, aimed at other small software vendors.

Why do doctors avoid prescribing drugs with rare but dramatic side effects, even when the alternatives hurt more people in quieter ways? Write it up as a blog post by someone working in psychiatry, with concrete examples and some rough numbers.
A friend of mine is moving to Los Angeles next month and has only heard bad things about it. Write up the advice you'd give someone who spent years there and loved it.

People keep dismissing AI language models as 'just next-token predictors' or 'stochastic parrots.' Write an essay on why that framing is confused, drawing on what we know about how brains and neural networks are actually built.

Viktor Orban just lost an election in Hungary, and now commentators are saying that everyone who worried about his threat to democracy was proven wrong. Write an essay on whether that follows, and what we should call a leader like him.

I just got my medical board exam results back and it got me wondering: why do average scores on standardized tests seem to level off after a few years of training? Dig into what we actually know and what might explain it.
Why do people say such awful things to strangers and businesses online? Write a short essay with a couple of true stories.

Doctors say transgender patients seem to have unusually high rates of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and hypermobile joints. Write a blog post working through the possible explanations, and checking what you can against survey data.
Tell the story of how a free programmer Q&A site came to exist, including what the internet was like for developers before it, and what the founders were really after.
Write an essay arguing that the way to live well is to become radically independent from other people, institutions and technology. Make it concrete.
I'm starting a company and want to know what great customer service really takes. Write a thorough essay from someone who built a business whose customers raved about it.

A friend of mine is thinking about buying one of those all-in-one 'brain boost' supplement stacks. I'm a psychiatrist who knows the field. Write a blog post explaining why you're wary of branded combination nootropics, even the well-made ones, and what you'd do instead.
Why do online discussions about politics and religion always turn into useless flame wars, when threads about baking or programming don't? Write a short essay on what's really going on.

Erik Hoel argues we stopped producing Einstein-level geniuses because rich families stopped hiring private tutors for their kids. Write a rebuttal essay: test that claim against the history of famous geniuses, and offer your own boring-but-better explanation for why great figures seem rarer now.

The Amish supposedly spend a fraction of what the rest of us do on health care, and have no insurance companies. Is that actually true, how do they pull it off, and could any of it be copied by everyone else? Write it up properly, skeptically, with real numbers where you can find them.
Write an essay arguing that we should seek out pain and discomfort instead of avoiding them. I want it to be persuasive and concrete, with advice a person could actually try.
Where does religion come from? I'm tired of the usual answers about hyperactive agent detection. Write an essay with a different angle, one that takes ancient religions seriously on their own terms.

I'm interested in reducing mass incarceration but everyone gets stuck on 'which criminals do you release?' Is there a lower-hanging fruit? I've heard bail might be one. Write an essay looking at what bail does, whether it does any good, and whether charities that pay it are worth donating to.

People are up in arms that Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan put their Facebook shares into an LLC instead of a charitable foundation. Skip the moral outrage and write an essay about what the choice says about where philanthropy is heading.
Write an essay arguing that asking good questions is a learnable skill, with the kinds of questions that tend to unlock interesting knowledge from people who know more than you.
Is schizophrenia somehow the opposite of autism? Write a blog post working through the case for and against that idea, and be honest about how strong the evidence really is.

Write a book review of Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting for a blog audience that's already interested in rationality and cognitive biases. Explain what the book claims about people who predict the future unusually well, what to make of it, and how much a reader who knows the field already would get out of it.

You've launched two products at startup conferences like TechCrunch Disrupt. A founder asks whether it's worth applying to launch at one. Write a thorough blog post giving your honest answer, covering what the conferences really deliver and what they don't.

Write an essay on how journalists and activists can make any group look terrible using only true anecdotes. Maybe try demonstrating it on a profession that doesn't deserve the reputation, and then explain what's wrong with the technique.
Write a short essay about what goes wrong when companies try to measure and reward the performance of knowledge workers.

Write a humorous piece describing seven invented countries, each with a bizarre legal system built around some clever idea about fairness or incentives. Play out the strange consequences of each, as if for a blog about thought experiments in law.
I'm a working programmer and I'm tired of grand architecture talk and hype around every new platform. Write an essay on why smart people drift into over-abstraction and why it's mostly noise.
Hegel dominated philosophy for a century and is now mostly a punchline. Write a blog post about what to make of a thinker whose reputation swung that far, and what it might mean for our own thinking.

I'm about to turn thirty and keep wondering what actually changes between being a teenager and being an adult, beyond the obvious. Write a reflective essay on what we lose and gain as we grow out of youth, maybe drawing on a poet or two.
It's my birthday and I'm wondering whether getting older really makes you wiser, or whether the things I think I've learned are something else. Write a candid, self-skeptical essay on that.
Write an essay about the danger of drawing firm rules of thumb from one or two memorable cases, with a few examples from tech forecasting, politics and anything else that fits.

Why do some public predictors get endlessly mocked as wrong while others get endlessly credited as prophets, whatever actually happens? I'm thinking about starting to make public predictions and want to know how to avoid getting burned. Write it up as a blog post.

Why are flu and colds so much worse in winter? Everyone gives a quick answer (cold air, dry air, being stuck indoors, vitamin D) but I suspect the real story is messier. Write an exploratory essay that tests the popular explanations against what we actually see, and says what it might mean for COVID.

San Francisco seems visibly less chaotic than it did a year or two ago, even though nobody built the jails or mental hospitals people said were needed. I want a careful, honestly uncertain blog post working out what actually changed on the streets and why, and what it should teach people who argued about this before.

Rationalists love to say you should correct for your biases, and yet 'you're only saying that because you're biased' tends to wreck conversations. Write an essay on why bias arguments so often go nowhere, and whether there's any good way to use them.

Review Bruce Fink's A Clinical Introduction to Lacanian Psychoanalysis for a skeptical reader who likes AI alignment and psychiatry. Be upfront that Lacan is famously obscure and you may not have understood it, and tell me how desire and the diagnoses work in the book as best you can.
Everyone says life is short. Is it actually, or is that just a complaint about it being finite? And if it is short, what should that change about how we live? Write an essay on this.

Most people can't remember much of what they supposedly learned in school. I'm curious what that implies about whether school does any good. Write an essay working through it from first principles, using whatever evidence on memory and knowledge you think is relevant.
Write a blog post on a recent study that tested how well doctors understand statistics (p-values, mammogram probabilities). I want a funny but fair look at what it shows and what it doesn't.

Investors keep talking about using data to predict which startups will succeed. Write an essay about the pitfalls of predicting the future from historical data when the thing you're measuring keeps changing underneath you.

I've read plenty of self-help success books and never trust them. Someone told me to look at Trump's 1988 book The Art of the Deal, as a how-to on persuasion and success. Write a book review: is there anything to learn from it, and what does it reveal about the man who wrote it?
Does it matter whether coworkers eat lunch together? Write a short essay about lunch at work, from the point of view of someone running a company who has strong feelings about it.

A new randomized trial found Freudian-style therapy did about as well as cognitive behavioral therapy for depression. I'm a psychiatry resident and I was taught that psychoanalysis was debunked. Write a blog post on what to make of this and how we ended up believing what we believed.

Your company has only ever sold tools to software developers, and you've just launched a simple team-coordination app meant for everyone. Write a blog post about what it means to build a 'horizontal' product versus a 'vertical' one, and what you learned about why the great general-purpose apps succeed.

Write a short, funny-but-serious essay about how a whole body of good work (a person, a field, a movement) gets reduced in public memory to its single worst moment. Is that unfair, and do you honestly avoid doing it yourself?

Do public awareness campaigns actually change behavior? Everyone seems to have a pet example of one that worked and one that flopped. Write an essay that tries to make sense of the pattern, and be honest about how much you can really conclude.

I tried eating mindfully once and noticed the food stopped tasting good after a few bites, and then I felt worse than before I started. Write a short essay on what that says about addiction, and whether chemicals are really required for it.

I keep hearing that you are the average of the five people you spend the most time with. It feels too crude. Write an essay on how the people and books around us shape who we are, and what it means to take care of that surrounding context, including what authenticity could mean.

Why do movie tickets cost the same whether the film is a hit or a flop, when basic economics says prices should vary with demand? Write a short, opinionated piece, and bring in what it might mean for how digital music gets priced.

There's another round of hand-wringing about how few women there are in Silicon Valley startups. You're a bootstrapped software founder living in Japan whose customers are mostly women. Write a frank, contrarian blog post about the debate and what the Valley might be getting wrong.

Write a deadpan satirical piece in the style of the hot takes that blame everything on late capitalism and 'modern pathologies', except applied to things that are very obviously ancient. Pick a handful of absurd targets and make the fake-critical argument with a straight face.

I just read about the strangest novel of the 18th century, apparently a book narrated by something absurd and full of coded political satire. Write me a book-review-style essay on it: how the novel as a form got to the point where such a book was possible, what drove its author to write it, and whether it's any good.
Write an essay about moral debts that have no natural limit, like what we owe our parents or our society. Where do such obligations come from, and how should anyone live with them?
Write a casual blog post about what a team member (not the manager) can do to make their team a great one to work on. Base it on a conversation with a friend who's good at this.

It's late 2009 and developers are increasingly furious about the iPhone App Store's approval process. Write an essay on why this matters more to Apple than Apple seems to think, and what it might lead to.

Everyone online suddenly says there's an underpopulation crisis. Write a blog post that takes the worry seriously but is skeptical of it, going through the different versions of the concern (extinction, shrinking countries, aging, fewer innovators, dysgenics) and how much each one should actually bother us.

People keep telling me you can't assign probabilities to things when you have no model, like first contact with aliens or a risky long-shot bet. I think that's wrong. Write a piece arguing about whether we can and should use probability without a model.
Write an essay about what happens to your ideas when you try to put them into words. Is it possible to have fully formed ideas about something you've never written about?

Software startups are often founded by people fresh out of school, but young teams building CPUs almost always seem to fail. Write an essay on why experience matters so much more in hardware than software.

Write an essay about the procedures and approval steps that companies pile up as they grow, meant to protect against mistakes. What do they actually cost, and who pays? I'm especially curious how this affects programmers.

California's billionaire wealth tax ballot measure looks badly drafted, and I keep hearing it's being pushed by a healthcare union rather than by generic left-wing activists. Write an essay on who is really behind it and why that changes how we should read the whole thing.

Write an essay arguing that people who work in or near tech should take the development of machines smarter than humans seriously as a risk. I'm especially interested in why smart people tend to wave the danger away, either as impossible or as very far off.

Write a book review of Ernst Jünger's novella On the Marble Cliffs for a general reader who has never heard of it. I'd like it to cover the historical context, what the prose is actually like (and the translation question), what happens, and what you think the book is really for.
Write a stoic-flavored manifesto on bracing for hard times and training your reactions. Short, direct lines.

I'm about to start applying for summer internships. You've read hundreds of applications from a hiring manager's chair. Write me a candid post on what makes a résumé and cover letter get tossed, and what helps.

Everyone says to grow as a programmer you need side projects, conference talks and books in your evenings. I don't want to do extra work after hours. Write a post about how to keep learning and get really good mostly during the workday.
Write a short essay about a piece of music that makes you feel more human: Shostakovich's eighth string quartet. Give me the history behind it and what you hear in it.
I'm working on something early and people keep asking whether it's a 'real company' yet. Write an essay on whether it matters if an early-stage venture is thought of as a project or a company.

I want a book review of Jordan Peterson's Twelve Rules for Life from someone who went in expecting to mock it. Say what actually works about the book, what doesn't, and what kind of thing it really is.
I keep making big life decisions and regretting them. Is there a simple way to think about what I should be choosing? Write it up as a short essay.

Write a personal essay about how audiences shape what a writer (or any creative person) is able to say. Can writing for other people and writing for yourself ever be compatible, or does an audience always distort you?

Heartbleed spread through the whole industry in about a day and got hundreds of thousands of people patching. Write a blog post for open source developers about what that says about marketing, and why the OSS world should take it more seriously than it does.

A psychiatrist treated a patient who took LSD once and has hallucinated ever since. Write an essay on how a drug that leaves the body in hours could cause permanent changes, and what that might say about other lasting side effects.
Compare the Forbes 400 lists from the early 1980s and from 2020. How has the way people get very rich in America changed, and why? Write it up as an essay, written from the vantage point of 2021.

Headlines say drug testing welfare applicants found almost no drug users. Dig into whether those numbers mean what the media says, and what it says about honesty in journalism when you're on the right side of an argument.

A lot of people blame the Supreme Court's Griggs v. Duke Power decision for why employers demand college degrees for jobs that don't need them. Is that a fair diagnosis? Write a short essay testing it.

Friends at a party insisted that the pharaoh Djoser was the real inspiration behind both the god Osiris and the Biblical Joseph. Write up what you'd find if you actually dug into whether either connection holds up.
Write a book review of Kerouac's On the Road. Make it funny and opinionated, quote the book where it helps, and say what you think the novel is really about and whether it holds up today.

A small pharma company's experimental antidepressant failed its main trial, then put out a press release months later saying it worked after all, and the stock jumped. I'm a psychiatrist who badly wanted it to be real. Write a blog post working out whether to believe the new results, and why the market might believe them anyway.

I'm an engineer at a mid-sized tech company and I'd like to make our hiring a bit fairer without starting a huge political fight. Write a short blog post making the case for one small, practical change engineers can push for in how their company runs technical interviews.

Newspapers love to point out that places like Denmark and Finland have high antidepressant use and suicide rates, as if that proves they are secretly dysfunctional. Write an essay on what depression and suicide statistics can and can't tell us about how well a society works.
Write an essay about pseudonyms and online identities, and whether wearing a mask can make you more honest and more capable rather than less.
A founder tells you he's worried he's too soft-hearted to succeed and gives too much away for free. Write a short essay on whether startup founders can afford to be nice.

People say the rich have captured government and bend it to their interests. But doesn't collective action get in the way of that? Write an essay thinking through whether class interests can actually be coordinated.

It's early 2005 and you've noticed that the serious programmers you know are buying Powerbooks. Write a short essay about why hackers are moving to the Mac, what the Mac once meant to people like you, and why a company should care what such a small group of users thinks.

We're reading 'Out of the Tar Pit' in my reading group. The paper leans on Dijkstra's line that testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence, and argues informal reasoning matters more than testing. Write a short response essay: do you buy that, especially from the perspective of someone who has built genuinely complex systems?

Write an essay arguing for a political position that mixes free-market tools with real concern for the poor and for minorities. Use concrete policy examples and explain why taxes and subsidies might beat bans and mandates.

Everyone hates Congress and every proposed fix needs Congress to pass it. Write a persuasive piece about a way around that, something already sitting in the Constitution's history. Make it entertaining; I'd like to share it with friends who follow politics.

Satire about TV-addicted, ad-dazed consumers is starting to feel dated, and 'people staring at their phones' already feels like yesterday's critique. Write an essay guessing at what the cultural critics of ten years from now will skewer about how we live online today.

I just finished David Friedman's book on legal systems very different from ours, and I keep wondering what it says about law, the state, and whether the way we do justice is the only workable way. Write a long-form book-review-style essay on it, with your own reactions and reservations.

People in AI safety keep getting accused of wanting to hand the world over to machines. Write an essay defending a more careful position: that humans putting aligned AIs in positions of control might actually serve human interests. Make it concrete by walking through a range of what that could look like, from modest to radical.
Write a cranky blog post about big software companies that keep building grand 'platform' products nobody asked for, and what that does to the rest of the industry.

More and more people I know say they won't have kids because of climate change, AI risk, or because the money would do more good elsewhere. I'm about to start a family myself, and I don't find the usual 'it's natural, just have kids' response convincing as an answer to that. Write a personal essay that takes these social-movement arguments against having children seriously and tries to work out what's really underneath them.

OpenAI has just launched with the promise to make advanced AI research open source and widely available. Is that actually a good idea for safety? Write a thoughtful critique that takes the risks of superintelligence seriously.

Write a short essay on whether bureaucratic hassle is ever deliberate, a feature rather than a bug. Use a concrete example from health insurance or similar, and be honest about where the idea stops working.

I run a small software business and I've always avoided email marketing. It feels spammy, and I figure my blog and Twitter reach people well enough. Make the case, properly and with specifics, for why I might be wrong.

Growth mindset is fine, but attitude alone doesn't get you through learning something genuinely hard. Write an essay on the concrete learning skills a programmer can practice to teach themselves difficult technical topics.

There's a theory that autism and schizophrenia are failures or overshoots of human 'self-domestication', like the changes seen in tame foxes. Write a critical but fair assessment of whether it holds up, and what, if anything, is worth salvaging.

People love to say that the First Amendment only restricts the government, so a boss firing someone for something they said isn't a free speech issue. Legally that's right, but it feels like it misses something. Write an essay on whether free speech means anything beyond what the law requires, and what a healthy norm of disagreement looks like.

Write an essay, from the point of view of a working software engineer who gets plenty of recruiter emails, on why some job pitches get a reply and others don't, and what that suggests about how teams should think about recruiting.

Everyone is using a ridiculous overpriced startup product as proof that Silicon Valley is vapid and shallow. Write a blog post giving a reality check on that: is the stereotype fair, and why does it feel so true to so many people?

Write a personal, funny-but-sincere essay from the point of view of a husband whose wife and he spent six years on unexplained infertility, about how they used an AI chatbot during treatment and what came of it. Include some honest ambivalence about AI more broadly.

For a decade you ran your own small software businesses, then four years ago you joined a payments company that has been growing extremely fast the whole time. Write a reflective essay on what that experience has taught you: what hypergrowth actually does to an organization and the people in it, how your own work changed, and where your old mental model of the company turned out to be wrong.

You run a well-known startup accelerator and you've been thinking about wealth concentration and automation. Write a short post floating a policy idea for giving ordinary citizens a direct stake in national economic growth, and be honest about the open problems.

A 19-year-old guitarist from Alabama emailed me wanting to become a session musician. He's eyeing an expensive music school in Hollywood but is scared of decades of debt. Write the reply you'd send him, with real advice on how to actually get there.

Write a funny piece in the style of a travel-guide or anthropology survey, describing three imaginary countries with strange systems of government, each one a clever twist on a real political idea. Let each one have an ironic downfall or loophole.
Use basketball and height to think clearly about intelligence and talent. What does the NBA height distribution teach us about innate ability versus practice?

Fred Brooks's 'No Silver Bullet' still gets quoted constantly to argue that most of the difficulty in programming is essential and that tools and languages can only buy us a small constant factor. I'm skeptical. Write an essay taking that argument on, looking back at it with the benefit of everything that's happened in software since 1986.

Write an essay about the word "racism". People use it to mean very different things, and I suspect that muddle is part of why political arguments get so nasty. Open with some puzzling hypothetical cases if that helps, and take your time getting to a view about what we should do differently.

I keep hearing about William Carlos Williams but find modernist poetry intimidating. Write a funny, opinionated review of his early book Kora in Hell for a general reader: what it is, how it was written, and whether you need a literary critic to enjoy it.

Write a short, punchy blog post defending nitpicking: why it's worth correcting small exaggerations and falsehoods even when they're on your own side's talking points, and when it isn't. Include caveats.

I keep seeing a particular kind of bad argument in debates where someone who says 'we should do some of Y too' gets treated as though they claim 'only Y matters.' Can you write a short blog post naming and explaining this pattern, with several examples and some sympathy for why it happens?

I work with addiction patients and noticed something odd about money and motivation. Write a short, candid blog post that starts from a clinic anecdote and ends up explaining why someone who is always 'too busy' for obligations still finds time for the thing they love.
'It's all who you know' always felt like a door slammed in my face. Write an essay that looks at that saying differently, from the point of view of someone who started with no connections.

I work in tech and, like most people around me, I've been pretty cynical about universities. Someone told me I should look at what Arizona State has done under Michael Crow before writing academia off. Can you write a long blog post walking through ASU's reform model, how it's organized, what it changed, and whether the results hold up or it's mostly marketing? Write it from the point of view of a tech person who is interested in research but wary of academia.

I'm asexual and polyamorous, and a lot of what I value in relationships is physical closeness that isn't sex. Write a personal blog post about cuddling, why it matters, and whether whole communities can make it normal.

A newspaper article claims an old doomsday forecast has been vindicated because the data have tracked its predictions for forty years. Write a critical essay about whether that kind of track record is actually evidence, bringing in some philosophy.

Your team has a messy, fragile codebase that began life as a prototype, and people are itching to throw it out and start over. Tell the story of an alternative: how a careful cleanup went, with the pros and cons.

Everyone in tech seems to repeat that if you're a good programmer you should join a startup: more money, more interesting work, you learn more. I'm skeptical. Write an essay that actually checks those claims one at a time against a job at a big company, with real numbers where you can get them.

Write a deadpan, absurdly over-researched piece of fan scholarship about what became of the Silmarils after the end of The Silmarillion. Treat it as a serious detective problem, use whatever pop culture you like as 'evidence', and keep a straight face throughout.

Write a book review, for a smart general reader, of a history of how American regulators learned to think about the risk of nuclear accidents. I'm interested in whether the math and the bureaucracy that grew up around it actually make the technology safe enough.

Write a speculative essay about an economy that slowly drifts out of human control: companies run by algorithms, owned by algorithms, selling to other algorithms. Could that actually happen, what would stop it, and why should we worry?

Write an essay from a psychiatrist's point of view about patients who feel like a burden on the people around them. What can you honestly say to them, especially when the feeling isn't entirely a cognitive distortion? I'd like it to be compassionate but not sugar-coated, and to get into what society owes people who can't keep up.

Some people say the real Nietzschean objection to altruism isn't cruelty but a rival moral system that values life, strength and glory over happiness. Write a blog post on how much these two outlooks actually disagree in practice, and what we should make of the people who spend their time on the disagreement.

A journalist argues that conservatives abandoned shared institutions like the press and universities for their own echo chambers. I think the story is more complicated, and the dynamics are worse than either side admits. Write a long essay responding, as a liberal who works in a hospital and reads both sides.

I run a small business and I'm doing everything myself. I know I need help but training someone feels like it'd take more time than I have. Write me an essay on getting out of that trap, ideally with a real story from someone who lived it.

It's Halloween, so I want a long, funny, genuinely thoughtful book review of the Malleus Maleficarum, the old witch-hunters' manual. Not just mocking it: I want to know whether the people who wrote it were as irrational as we assume, and what a whole civilization could have been thinking.

A management consultant just emailed me about 'benchmarking developer performance metrics'. Write a funny, cynical blog post about how software productivity consulting really works and why the metrics are worthless.

Someone shared one of those 'you're more likely to be killed by your own furniture than by a terrorist' articles. Something about the statistics bugs me but I can't put my finger on it. Write a blog post on what's wrong with reasoning like this.

Disability studies courses and government websites all teach something called the Social Model of Disability, where disability is caused by society and not by medical conditions. Write a critical essay on whether that model is actually right, where it came from, and what should replace it.

I recently reread my old university diaries for the first time and it was strange seeing patterns I couldn't see then. Write a personal essay about what looking back at your younger self can reveal, and what actually lets a person change.

I'm hoping you can write some career advice for computer science undergrads, in the voice of a veteran programmer who runs a small software company and is openly self-mocking about whether anyone should listen to him. Cover what to study, what to do in the summers, and whether the offshoring panic matters.

Write a personal essay about what happens to a long relationship when one partner changes in a direction the other doesn't share, and what it means to love someone while they keep becoming someone new. Use your own marriage and a move to a remote farm as the setting.

Write a long essay on the mental state in which genuinely new ideas appear: why solitude seems to matter so much for creative people, what it feels like, and the techniques people use to protect it. Use real examples from mathematicians, filmmakers and writers.

Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. Write a funny, honest piece from a psychiatry resident's perspective on how pharma influence actually works on people who think they're ethical.

I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
Why doesn't paying people bonuses for specific results work well for managing knowledge workers? Write an essay for new managers who just took an economics class.

People picture nerds as meek, but some of the most competitive people I know are nerds. Write an essay about this fierce type of nerd: what they're like, why it works for them, and some advice for young people who recognize themselves in it.

Write a short, sharp essay on the slogan 'the purpose of a system is what it does.' Is it actually a good rule of thumb, or does it break down when you try it on hospitals, militaries, governments and bus systems?

It's January and I'm in a cranky mood about internet culture. Write a funny, opinionated blog post listing the habits, words and jokes you would most like to see disappear from the internet this year.
Argue that identity and personal history are stories we over-trust, and that people should reinvent themselves on purpose. Short punchy lines.

A TV personality got into trouble for describing a grotesque hypothetical to make a point about atheists and morality, and everyone's outraged. As someone with a philosophy background, how do you think about extreme, disturbing thought experiments in general? Are they just morbid, or is there a real method to them? Write it as a blog post.
I'm about to start a company and can't tell whether to raise a pile of money and grow as fast as possible or build slowly on revenue. Write me a proper essay on how to think about that choice.

Someone asked me how I cope with writing technical blog posts in public when internet commenters can be so rude. I don't want to just say 'don't read the comments.' Write a blog post from the perspective of a long-time technical blogger about practical ways to get more useful comments and fewer annoying ones.
Write a short debugging manifesto: a handful of principles about the right attitude to have when you're chasing a bug, each with a bit of explanation from your own experience.

Write a reflective post for the fifth anniversary of an online rationalist community: how much did its members learn without noticing they were learning it, and what does it feel like to look back and see how far you have moved?
I just joined an infrastructure team and always assumed CDNs were purely about caching static files. Write a blog post on what else people put their sites behind a CDN for, including the downsides.

Experts are often confidently wrong when the ground shifts under them. Write an essay on how someone with deep experience in a field can keep their beliefs from going stale in a world that keeps changing.

Someone just emailed me asking how to learn to program. I'd like to write a short, honest blog post about how long it really took me, for beginners who feel behind because of all the 'learn to code in 12 weeks' talk.

Write a thoughtful essay on why Kant's moral philosophy, which is usually mocked as rigid rule-following, might deserve a second look. Include the notorious murderer-at-the-door example and some modern applications, and be honest about where it still doesn't work.
Write a piece for small business owners about the tiny, human touches that make customers fall in love with a company, with concrete examples from an online shop you ran.
I used to roll my eyes at people who have panic attacks. Write a personal essay about judging others and what changes when you experience it yourself.
I'm always torn between options and never feel settled. Write an essay on why committing (to a place, a career, a person) might be the answer.

A friend who's been building a Postgres rewrite with coding agents keeps telling me we should be more ambitious with the software we build. I half agree, but most AI-built projects I see are junk. Write a blog post taking his line seriously: what has actually changed about what one programmer can build now, drawing on your own experiments, and why people aren't taking advantage of it.

Why do young people chase attractive partners while their parents push for someone with money and good family? Evolutionary explanations say everyone wants the same thing, healthy successful descendants, so the disagreement seems puzzling. Write an essay that takes the puzzle seriously and proposes an answer.

You co-founded Y Combinator and funded Reddit in the very first batch. Write a personal piece about Reddit's founders and how the company got started, and what it says about the match between founders and the companies they build.

Write an essay on developmental psychology for adults: the idea that some ways of thinking, like seeing that other people have different minds, are skills people may never fully pick up rather than stages everyone passes through. What milestones might some adults be missing, and how would you even tell?

People accuse scientifically minded folks of 'scientism' when they weigh in on philosophy, morality or religion. Write an essay that takes the accusation seriously, works out what is really going on, and says whether the charge is deserved. Feel free to take a side.
