I'm a working web developer and I keep hearing people argue about whether browsers should follow web standards strictly or keep supporting old, sloppy pages. Write me a long blog post that explains why standards are so hard to get right in practice, and why a browser team can't win either way.
Write a blog post giving a quick, irreverent checklist for judging how good a software team is, with a sentence or two of justification for each item.
You asked programmers on Twitter what made a bug feel 'impossible' to understand and got hundreds of replies. Write a post that sorts those reasons into categories.

Write a blog post about the link between smoking and schizophrenia. I've seen claims that smoking causes psychosis and others that it protects against it, and I'd like someone to dig into how good the evidence on each side actually is, and what researchers should do when studies disagree.

You've spent years doing office hours with early-stage startups. Write an essay about the question you find more useful than "how can this company make more money": how could it become more powerful? Cover the different forms that takes and what limits it.

People keep saying content moderation on big platforms would be easy if the moderators just used common sense. I think that's wrong, but I want to make the case with something more than vibes. Write an essay on why large platforms can't come up with moderation rules that people agree on, using David Turner's "No Vehicles in the Park" game as a starting point.

Politicians keep saying the only way to become a billionaire is by exploiting people. You spent years at Y Combinator trying to pick the founders who would get enormously rich. Write an essay that uses what you actually looked for in YC interviews to answer that claim, and give founders honest advice on how to do well in the interview along the way.
Is there really such a thing as good taste, or is it all just preference? I'm giving a talk to a student debating society and want a short, rigorous argument for one side. Write it as an essay.

I keep hearing that lavender extract is a real treatment for anxiety, maybe even better than benzos. You're a psychiatrist who reads the literature skeptically. Write up whether the evidence holds up and what you'd actually tell a patient who wanted to try it.

I've lost my sense of curiosity lately. Nothing feels interesting, even though I'm not burned out. Write a personal essay about what it means to be curious, why it can dry up, and how you tell what is actually worth pursuing.

I've been thinking about the way people argue online and why so much of it never changes anyone's mind. Write a funny but sharp blog post classifying the different kinds of opinion-posts by what psychological need they serve for the writer and for the audience, rather than by topic.

It's 2004. You worked at Yahoo through the dot-com bubble and watched it burst. Everyone now treats anything that was fashionable in 1999 as discredited. Write an essay arguing about which of the bubble's ideas were actually right and will matter in the long run.

Write a speculative essay that treats ideas, not people, as the real actors in culture: creators as hosts that ideas use. What does that lens say about reputation, about why audiences trap successful artists in their old work, and about how a creator might keep some freedom?

Your daughter is turning eight and you wish you could hand her a book about living freely and getting things done. Write that essay: what does 'agency' really mean, what does it look like in the lives of people who have it (a filmmaker, perhaps), and what held you back from it for so long?

I want a blog post about what happens when you take utilitarianism seriously at a meetup and someone pushes you on animal welfare. How do you stay sane while still being honest about your own inconsistency?
Everyone says AI tutors are about to revolutionize education. Write an essay on whether that's actually going to happen, and what might stand in the way.

You've just built a website where people can experiment with DNS on a real subdomain and watch queries arrive live. Write a long blog post on why you made it, how the experiments were designed, what user testing taught you, and the interesting parts of building the backend.

It's mid-2013 and you run Y Combinator. You've been asked to give a talk to a room full of investors about where startup investing is heading over the next decade. Write the talk as an essay: what forces are changing the business, and what should investors do about them?
There's a line between healthy caution and fear that stops you from making necessary changes to code. Write a blog post about how fear makes programmers worse and what teams can do about it.

I just finished Stuart Russell's book on AI safety, Human Compatible, and I'm trying to decide what I think of it. Write a long review for a blog audience that already follows the AI risk debate: what the book does well, where its argument is strongest, and anything about its approach that gives you pause.

Airbnb just went public, and you funded them back in 2008 when nobody else would. Write a short piece for future founders about what was special about the Airbnb founders and how they got the company off the ground during Y Combinator.

Why does WiFi work so badly at tech conferences, even ones full of engineers? I'm helping organize an event for a few hundred people and want to understand what actually goes wrong and what to ask the venue. Write it up conversationally.
I'm thinking of quitting my tech job to take a year off with no plan. Write a personal post about why a self-funded sabbatical can be a good idea, drawing on your own experience taking one before.

Why is a byte 8 bits? Is that a historical accident or is there something genuinely best about 8? I'm not a computer historian, so write it as an honest investigation: lay out the plausible reasons, say which ones you find convincing and where you're unsure.

I design programming languages, but I don't think of it as research. Write an essay, adapted from a talk to language researchers, on what changes when you treat a programming language as a design problem rather than a research topic.

Write a dialogue between two friends arguing about whether eugenics deserves to be a permanent taboo. One thinks voluntary, non-coercive versions are fine to discuss and that the stigma is inconsistent, the other thinks some slopes really are slippery. I'd like history and a real comparison with another movement that did comparable harm, and I'd like it to end somewhere honest rather than tidy.

I want a blog-style book review of Peter Thiel's Zero to One, focusing on what he says about monopoly and whether competition is really as good as economics textbooks say. Skeptical but fair, please, with your own counterpoints.

Christopher Alexander just died. I know him vaguely as the architect behind A Pattern Language, but I'm more interested in what his ideas could mean for how a society passes knowledge between generations. Write a personal, reflective essay on that.

Write up a pricing case study for SaaS founders. The company is a server monitoring service that charged per server plus per website (roughly $11/server, cheaper at volume, $2/website), and its typical customer has about 7 servers. They A/B tested that against a grid of three or four plans starting at $99/month, segmented by users and support level. Trial signups were 150 vs 113 out of ~2,150 visitors each, cards added 23 vs 18, and new monthly revenue $420 vs $876. Explain why the old model was a mistake, what the results mean (including how far to trust them), and what other founders should take from it.
I just saw a newspaper piece arguing we shouldn't run experiments to test whether we live in a simulation, in case it gets the universe shut down. Write a short, funny-but-serious rebuttal.

Write a book review of David Sinclair's Lifespan for a skeptical, curious general reader. Explain his theory of why we age, what he thinks we can do about it, how other researchers see it, and whether ending aging would even be a good idea.

People keep claiming that environmentalism, social justice, transhumanism, even Apple fandom is 'really a religion'. Is that a meaningful claim or a cheap rhetorical move? Write an essay working out what, if anything, is going on.

I'm a psychiatrist and my patients can't find buspirone anywhere, and meanwhile insulin is absurdly expensive even though it's off-patent. Why do drug markets behave so differently from markets for bread or chairs? Write a blog post working through it, with some honesty about what you don't know.
Write an essay arguing that people should move across the world and weave themselves into many cultures, as a way to live well. Give it a playful but serious tone.

I'm trying to make up my mind about whether junior doctors who strike over their working conditions are justified. You trained in a medical system outside the US and have worked in the American one. Write something honest about what you saw and where you land, including your doubts about labor disputes in general.
I'm an individual engineer on a small team, so what I personally ship matters a lot. Write a blog post, personal rather than preachy, about the habits that actually help you get things done at work.

A prominent researcher argues that even if twin studies say schizophrenia is about 80% heritable, we shouldn't call it a genetic disease. Write a long essay responding, testing each objection against the standard we use when we say smoking causes lung cancer.

There's a popular view in software circles that when people behave badly you should never blame discipline or attitude, only fix the incentives and the process. I think that's overcorrected. Write an essay on how much company culture actually matters, next to incentives and process, for things like speed, debugging, quality and ownership, and what it means for someone choosing where to work.

People keep accusing groups they dislike of being an insular echo chamber that doesn't listen to outside criticism, and no amount of evidence ever seems to satisfy them. Write an essay on how that argument works, and how a person should actually decide whose critics deserve their time.
Take the shutdown menu in Windows Vista and use it to write a short essay about what too many options does to people, and how you'd design your way out of it.

Whatever happened to the big public conversation about superintelligence and AI risk from ten years ago? I'd like a thoughtful book-review-style essay that also looks at an alternative picture of how advanced AI might develop, and whether the old worries still hold up.

My Java programs at my old job were always slow and everyone blamed the language. Write a short blog post on whether Java is really a slow language, and what someone in that situation should do about it.

A blogger argues that since humanity may last 300,000 years or more and one person lives about a hundred, we should be very skeptical of anyone who thinks their own lifetime is special, whether because of a coming singularity or an apocalypse. Write a rebuttal that actually does the probability properly.
Write a punchy essay arguing that the way to learn fastest is to deliberately make a huge number of mistakes.

There's an old, much-repeated claim that Apple's research proved the mouse is faster than the keyboard and that keyboard users are fooling themselves. Write a blog post that looks at where that claim actually comes from, whether the evidence holds up, and what you find when you time some everyday editing tasks yourself.

Lately it's fashionable to say psychiatry lied to the public with the 'chemical imbalance' theory of depression. You're a psychiatry resident who thinks that charge is mostly unfair. Write a long essay defending your profession and explaining what the phrase actually meant and why it was said.

A big study just made headlines claiming childhood bullying causes terrible adult outcomes decades later, even after controlling for confounders. I'm skeptical of 'controlled for confounders' as a method. Write a blog post on whether we should believe results like this.

I just finished a biography of John von Neumann and I want to write about it properly. Not a plot summary: what was he actually like, where did someone like him come from, and what do we make of the man behind the legends? Write it as a thoughtful book review.

I went to a secular solstice event with a bunch of nerds and loved it, even though plenty of people call that kind of thing cringeworthy. Write a blog post about why strong communities, religious or not, so often seem to depend on being a little embarrassing, and what that means for atheists trying to build one.

I've got a stack of local races and ballot measures coming up and I never feel informed enough on them. Write a blog post about whether it's actually sensible to use an AI model as a research assistant for deciding how to vote. Draw on a real attempt if you can, including how well it worked and where it went wrong.

Some tech people say it doesn't matter if AI eventually replaces humanity, as long as the successors are advanced. Should the future be human? Write an essay that takes both sides seriously and tells me what would make you comfortable handing the future to AI.

In high school I helped start an elaborate online role-play of an imaginary world that ended up running for more than a decade. Write a reflective essay about what years of simulated politics and worldbuilding can teach a person, including the odd, half-serious lessons about leadership.

What actually makes a company a startup, as opposed to just a new small business? Write an essay that gets to the bottom of it and follows the idea through to how it explains founders, investors and acquirers.
Someone from a big company's corporate development team wants to meet with our young, fast-growing startup. Write an essay for founders in this position: should they take the meeting?

Academics from privileged backgrounds often seem eager to blame their own group for the world's problems, which looks odd. Write a short essay proposing a psychological explanation that is charitable rather than cynical.

I'm a regular software engineer, not a manager, and I keep hearing that culture is set from the top. Write a blog post about whether individual engineers can actually change how things work at their company, drawing on concrete examples, and what tends to help when you try.

A headline is going around saying a new study proves trigger warnings are harmful to college students. Write a blog post for a skeptical general reader on whether the study shows that, and what you'd actually do about trigger warnings.
Write a funny personal essay about life with toddler twins, the kind where everything is a crisis. Early mornings, songs, bedtime, the whole chaos.
A 19-year-old who wants to do something great asks you whether to stay in college, join a company or start their own. Write your honest advice as a blog post.

I'm a medical resident, and I want to write something honest about what dying in a modern hospital is actually like, as opposed to the peaceful deathbed people imagine, and what I think should change about how we approach the end of life. Write it as a blunt, darkly funny, personal essay.

Windows and Unix can do basically the same things these days, so why do programmers on each side seem to think so differently? Write a thoughtful essay on the cultural divide between the two camps, where it comes from, and whether either is simply right.

For years people talked about computers and TV "converging." Write an essay on how that contest actually played out, why it went the way it did, and what it means for TV networks and anyone thinking of competing with them.

I just saw a headline claiming psychiatric treatment might increase suicide risk, based on a study showing treated people die by suicide far more often than untreated people. Write a piece on what's wrong with reading causation into numbers like that, with a sense of humor if you can manage it.

A lot of political arguments, about violent media, stereotypes, diversity training, rape culture and so on, lean on findings from social psychology. Write a skeptical but fair essay on how much weight those findings can bear, and try it by turning the usual arguments upside down.
Write an essay arguing that the wisest way to live is to do nothing: to not act, not react, not decide. Make the case as persuasively as you can.

Why do social movements like libertarianism, feminism or atheism end up as a loose cloud of NGOs rather than anything like a Church? Write an essay on how you would design an organization to capture a movement's energy, what the Catholic Church gets right, and why almost nobody copies it.
Write a book review of a popular-level book on quantum computing from the point of view of someone who isn't a mathematician and only half understood it, but still came away with one big picture.

Write an essay about whether it's ethical to publicize small hidden communities, both physical places like an undiscovered town and online subcultures that would rather stay obscure. When does sharing a discovery become exploiting it?

I've been watching a friend burn out on dating apps, and it got me thinking about how we go about choosing people in general, whether partners or colleagues. Write a short, personal essay on a different way to approach meeting and evaluating people.
Why doesn't the brain just spiral into endless bliss the moment it feels something good? Write a short blog post on that puzzle, and bring in whatever you know about advanced meditation.

I just lost a day at work to a bug caused by Ruby's Timeout. Write a blog post explaining how Timeout works under the hood, why it's dangerous, and how other languages have dealt with the same idea of killing a thread from the outside.

I know almost nothing about the technical side, but I've been following the AI risk debate. Do the recent advances in neural networks change how we should think about superintelligent AI as a goal-maximizing agent? Write an exploratory essay.
Write about a teacher who changed your life in only a few lessons. I want to give it to some of my students and their parents.

You've built a research career without an undergrad degree or a PhD, and teenagers keep emailing to ask whether they should skip university. Write the essay you wish you could send them: how to think about the decision, and the costs and pressures that come with not going, including the ones nobody warns you about.

Why do horoscope-style personality descriptions feel so uncannily accurate? I'd like a short essay that goes beyond 'they're vague' and asks what it would mean if those statements are true of almost everyone, and what we could learn from that.
Why is coming up with genuinely new ideas so hard, and why do so many of them show up in dreams or by accident? Write a short, speculative blog post.

I've been reading Bostrom's Superintelligence and got stuck on the idea of a hyper-competitive Malthusian future full of digital agents where consciousness might get optimized away. Write something speculative about whether anything meaningful could survive in that kind of economy, and where it might hide.

I have a five-year-old and I keep wondering how I'll ever explain the internet to her, and honestly how I should be using it myself. Write a thoughtful blog post on using the internet well, as something you get better at over time rather than something that just happens to you.

I just got back from a talk on effective charity where one of the speakers argued that donors are mostly fooling themselves. Write me a blog post about what it's like to hear that, and whether the idea of investing your money now and giving it away later actually holds up. Do some back-of-the-envelope math.

Perf review season is coming and I have to write peer reviews for coworkers I think are great. Everything I write comes out as 'X is awesome, love working with them.' Can you write a blog post on how to write positive feedback in a review that's actually useful to the person and to their managers?

I want a book-review style blog post about the Baumol effect as an explanation for why health care and education keep getting more expensive. Lay out the case, then say honestly what still bothers you.
Write a manifesto for someone who wants to live entirely in the future: always chasing what's newest and next. Make the case sincerely, as if you believed it.
Udemy vs Skillshare, Uber vs Lyft: the same teachers, drivers and customers use all of them. Write up some thinking on what peer-to-peer businesses end up looking like once they reach scale.

Everyone seems to read the Great Filter as proof that humanity is doomed. Write an essay on whether that's right: which candidate explanations for the Fermi paradox actually hold up, and how scared should we be?

Write an exploratory blog post, from the point of view of an engineer at a tech company, about the open questions you have about open source: when to use it versus building your own, why companies pay people to write it, and how you're supposed to evaluate it. It's fine to raise more questions than you answer.

I just finished a book about Soviet economic planning and the mathematicians who tried to fix it. Write a long, thoughtful review that goes beyond the plot to what it teaches about planning, incentives and who ought to run a country.
Tech companies keep lobbying for easier immigration for programmers, and critics say we should just train more Americans instead. Write a short, punchy essay taking a side in that argument.
Write a practical piece on how to get real value out of attending a music industry conference, for someone who's about to go to their first one and tends to waste these things.

The New York Times just ran a piece on the Hearing Voices Movement, people with hallucinations who want them treated as normal rather than medicalized. You're a psychiatrist who has met some of them. Write a numbered-points blog post giving your honest, mixed take: where the movement has a point and where its critics (and the press coverage) do.
Write a blog post for startup founders about why automating every part of a business might be a mistake. Draw on your experience running an online store.

Is the placebo effect actually real? I keep hearing it's one of the most powerful forces in medicine, but I've also seen claims that it's overblown. Write up what the evidence really says and how you'd make sense of it.

I'm curious about applying evolutionary thinking to psychiatry, which seems like it should be a natural fit but rarely is. Write a thoughtful review of a book that tries it, covering what the theory is, how well it handles real psychiatric conditions, what it might mean for society, and where you stay skeptical.

You're a psychiatrist reflecting on your own habits. Write an essay on the two broad stances a doctor can take toward what patients say they want, taking them at their word versus looking for the real problem underneath, and which one you lean toward and why.

Is fixing every bug in your software actually the right goal? Write an essay for a small software company owner on how to decide which bugs are worth fixing, with practical ways to find out about them and put a number on it.

I've heard that gout is oddly common among famous, successful people, and that there might be a real biochemical reason for it. Write a skeptical but curious blog post on whether high uric acid could actually make you more accomplished.

Someone at a party told me that if a product could be better, a competitor would already have built the better version, so markets basically guarantee things work about as well as they can. That doesn't match my experience buying anything, as a consumer or as a company. Write an essay on why it's so hard to buy products and services that actually work well, and what that means for the build vs. buy decision.

I tried a Kaggle competition, landed nowhere near the leaderboard, and now I'm wondering if I'm just bad at machine learning. You do ML as your actual job. Can you write a blog post about how real-world machine learning work compares to Kaggle?

I keep seeing devs who just have the LLM write code and paste errors back to it until it works, without really thinking. Models are getting good enough that maybe that's fine? Is there any future where that approach actually pays off for them?
My mom says she raised me so I owe her everything, including taking care of her when she's old. How far does a debt like that actually go?
I sell my small software product both as a downloadable desktop app and as a web app. Is it actually worth keeping the desktop version around?
honest question: why do you think so few women want to join early-stage startups?
You run an accelerator that picks companies after a short interview. Why do funding rounds take months to close, and does it really have to be that way?
people always say 'greed is good' and it makes me cringe. is there any version of that claim that actually makes sense?
We're an early-stage startup and I honestly don't know what number we should be tracking or what 'good' looks like. How should we think about growth?
Two senior people on our open source project keep arguing about whether a section of the docs is clear. Each thinks their rewrite is better. How do you actually settle that kind of thing?
I just found out there are already a few companies doing basically what I want to build. Am I too late? Should I drop the idea?
if one country gets superintelligent AI a few months before its rival, why would that be dangerous? is there a historical analogy?
if I really can't model something, can't I just say I don't know and refuse to put a probability on it? like choosing between a safe grant and a wild long shot
Should a company care more about its customers than about its own survival?
what's the deal with over-abstracting things? why do clever people end up building vague 'general' systems that miss the point?
Should a small, very productive core team of a language like Julia slow down to add code review, tests and internal docs so outsiders can contribute more easily? Or is that not worth it?
how come people say anti-rape poster campaigns are proven effective? what's the evidence and is it any good?

Why does everyone complain about lag on tablets and VR headsets but nobody seems to care about keyboard-to-screen latency on a normal computer? Is keyboard input just inherently less sensitive to delay?
can you build a startup hub like Silicon Valley in another city, or is it a one-off? what would it actually take?
Do you think we actually understand deep learning yet, or is the field still pretty ad hoc? Write a few paragraphs on it.
How did Steven Pressfield finally manage to finish a book after years of calling himself a writer?
Why do some bloggers refuse to promote friends' projects? Explain it as if you were one of them.
I'm stuck in silver in Overwatch and everyone says you have to play DPS to climb out of low ranks. Is that actually true?
we can't match big-company salaries. what are some cheap ways to make employees feel valued and keep them from leaving?
Should I quit my job and start a company? I've been asking successful people for advice but it's all contradictory. Why?
Do you ever notice how your friend group doesn't look like the general population at all, even though you never chose it that way?
I feel completely unmotivated today, nothing seems worth doing. What should I do with a day like this?
Polls say a huge share of Americans would give a kidney to a stranger, yet almost nobody actually does. Why is the gap so enormous? Is everyone just lying?
Is the slippery slope argument ever a good reason to oppose something that seems reasonable on its own?
why are corporations so hard to regulate? they always seem to find a loophole
I've felt guilty for years about something I did when I was young. How reliable is my memory of it, really, and can I do anything about the past?
is there really that much money in US politics? how does it compare to other stuff we spend on

When I don't know which product to buy I just ask someone who works in that field. That's the sensible approach, right?
how do I become more of an independent thinker instead of just absorbing the views I grew up with?
why do you build tolerance to heroin but people with ADHD can apparently stay on Adderall for years? that always seemed weird to me
Tim Berners-Lee's web won, but I keep feeling like we ended up with the wrong kind of internet. Is there a real case that the web is shaped badly, as opposed to just being the thing that happened?
why do so many startup founders fail, and what do the ones who succeed have in common?
ok be honest, what's the deal with On the Road? is it actually any good?

How can an unknown artist convince a big company to eventually back them?

people throw around the word "liberalism" like it just means being a Democrat or loving free markets. what is it actually, historically?
why are prescription drugs in the US so wildly more expensive without insurance, and is there any trick for paying less out of pocket?

how do valuation and dilution work for an angel investor? if I put in $50k, what do I actually own and what happens to it in later rounds?

how do DMs work on Mastodon? are they actually private?
What is folie a deux, and how does it work if psychosis is supposed to be a biological illness?

What's the real difference between the economics of a B2C software company and a B2B one? I keep hearing that B2B companies benefit when their customers succeed but I don't get why that matters so much.
Why are yes/no questions supposedly a good way to learn from coworkers? Seems like you'd just get a yes or a no.
Where did the school system actually come from? People say it was built to make obedient factory workers, but is that true?
Can you explain the idea of memes as parasites that evolve? Use a real parasite's life cycle to make it concrete, and give me an example from politics.
why do people give such confident reasons for things they did, when the reason is obviously made up after the fact? is there actual research on this
if there was an advanced civilization during the Ice Age, what would they have eaten? Does the history of crops say anything about this?
What's the actual difference between money and wealth? People use the words interchangeably but I've heard they aren't the same thing.
